segments.text: A realistic possibility that she was going to return in time just on the basis of submitting multiple notes.
That's a factual, that's a factual determination.
You look at the evidence, going like, well, it kind of looks like she wasn't going to come.
I know what the documents say.
The documents say she was going to come to six, but it kind of feels like she's not.
Well, that feeling is a factual determination, which is what the district court said.
For some reason, there was some uncomfortableness with the continued leave.
I get it.
I don't own a business.
I have employees in my firm, but it's not my business.
But I get it.
Like, oh, I really don't like this.
But that's not his determination.
It's the jury's determination.
Okay, so with respect to the discrimination claim and accommodation claims, your main argument is that there's a tribal issue of fact.
Absolutely, but I'm addressing the narrow thing that we got from the district court.
I'm happy to discuss the other ones, which was my second part.
But if you have questions, well, I was going to ask, there's two other claims, right?
Yes, Your Honor.
Retaliation?
Yes.
And failure to engage meaning or whatever the term is, meaningfully in the interactive process.
Right, which from the evidence, I would argue, is undisputed that they ever did.
Because again, there was no interactive process.
They were just waiting for FMLA to run out.
They didn't go like, hey, your FMLA is right now.
I know under California law, we have to engage in the interactive process.
Can we get on a call to see what you can do?
Well, the district court said that she offered, she didn't offer anything.
Basically, other than more leave.
Well, that's also a factor determination because there's facts that she was going to come in, that she was talking to her own supervisor.
Who supervised testified?
I knew she wanted to come back on the 6th because I kept hearing about it.
And then someone told Ms.
Eagleman, and Ms.
Eagleman testified: hey, I heard I was being fired on April 5th.
There's a letter to that effect, also.
Don't know whether that was, they don't know, and we don't know whether that was delivered, but it exists on April 5th.
And she was told.
Hey, it turns out you were fired because it turns out your FMLA was gone.
Never mind the interactive process.
We're going to send you a letter later.
And that's what they did.
But the district court didn't get into that.
They just determined she couldn't work.
So, again, a factual determination.
What would have all NAVCARE knew?
And I keep repeating, all NAVCAR knew.
What about retaliation since you're running low on time?
Oh, yes.
With regards to retaliation,
It goes to the protect activity of the leave itself, and that there was discriminant retaliatory animus in the decision to really just get rid of her under the pretext that FMLA had run out.
But again, this all comes back to that is not.

A legitimate reason that is, in fact, a retaliate, excuse me, a discriminatory animus to just let someone else go because you happen to take your FMLA and now you run out under the Fair Employment and Housing Act.
Under the ADA, maybe it's different.
The rules are different under Title VII.
I understand that, but we're in California under the Fair Employment and Housing Act.
And just to address this a little bit more, there's this argument before I run out of time with regards to the undue hardship.
My client was not fired for performance.
That's when this stuff comes up.
She wasn't fired for performance.
And if it was an undue hardship, they wouldn't have given her the four prior FMLA leaks without an issue.
Four, with that, they kept bringing up.
And they testified: yep, we were able to cover her those four prior ones.
So, why is the fifth one an issue?
They can't explain that.
